profile.feeling: But – the everyday contrast word; it leaves the word order alone.

senses.def: really, indeed (particle of surprise: Das ist aber nett!)

examples.text: Das Auto ist schön, aber es ist teuer.
examples.tr: The car is nice, but it’s expensive.

examples.text: Ich bin müde, aber ich gehe zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: I’m tired, but I’m going to work.

examples.text: Es ist kalt. Wir gehen aber trotzdem spazieren.
examples.tr: It’s cold. But we’re going for a walk anyway.

examples.text: Das ist aber nett von dir!
examples.tr: That’s really kind of you!

synonyms.nuance: but, yet – takes the first place, verb follows (…, doch ist es teuer)
however – written style, can stand inside the clause
but rather – only after a negation (nicht heute, sondern morgen)

etymology.text: From Middle High German aber, aver, from Old High German aber, ābar, abur, avur, afur, from Proto-Germanic *aferą (“behind”). Compare Luxembourgish awer (“but”), Low German aver.

funFacts: aber once meant “again” – it survives in abermals (once again).
pitfalls: aber does not change the word order: …, aber es ist teuer (subject, then verb) – it stands before the clause, at “position 0”.
After a negation, “but (rather)” is sondern: Nicht der Bus, sondern der Zug.
subtleties: aber can also stand inside the clause: Es ist aber teuer. (= But it is expensive.)

profile.feeling: Because – the everyday reason word; it sends the verb to the end.

examples.text: Ich trinke Wasser, weil ich Durst habe.
examples.tr: I’m drinking water because I’m thirsty.

examples.text: Er bleibt zu Hause, weil er müde ist.
examples.tr: He’s staying at home because he’s tired.

examples.text: Warum kommst du nicht? – Weil ich arbeiten muss.
examples.tr: Why aren’t you coming? – Because I have to work.

synonyms.nuance: because, for – main-clause order, a little more written
since, as – often at the start: Da es regnet, …
you see – an adverb inside the second clause (Ich bleibe hier, ich bin nämlich müde)

etymology.text: From the accusative of Middle High German wīle (modern Weile), from Old High German wīla, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu, from Proto-Germanic *hwīlō.

funFacts: weil is the old word for “while” (die Weile – a while), like English while.
pitfalls: The finite verb goes to the END of the clause: …, weil ich Durst habe (not *weil ich habe Durst – heard in fast speech, but wrong in writing).
A comma always comes before weil.
subtleties: A weil-clause can come first; then the main clause starts with its verb: Weil ich müde bin, gehe ich nach Hause.
The answer to Warum? is a weil-clause on its own: Weil ich müde bin.

profile.feeling: Because, for – a reason in main-clause order; in questions a softening particle.

senses.def: then, so – particle in questions (Was ist denn los?)

examples.text: Ich trinke Wasser, denn ich habe Durst.
examples.tr: I’m drinking water, for I’m thirsty.

examples.text: Wir bleiben zu Hause, denn es ist kalt.
examples.tr: We’re staying at home because it’s cold.

examples.text: Wo bist du denn?
examples.tr: Where are you, then?

examples.text: Heute ist das wichtiger denn je.
examples.tr: Today that is more important than ever.

synonyms.nuance: because – verb at the end; more common in speech
since, as

etymology.text: From Middle High German denne, tenne, from Old High German denna, a variant of danne, from Proto-West Germanic *þan. Doublet of dann. The functional split between denn and dann was prescribed only by the grammarians of the 18th century. Cognate with English then and than.

funFacts: denn and dann were one word until 18th-century grammarians split their jobs – both are cousins of English then and than.
pitfalls: denn keeps main-clause order: …, denn ich habe Durst (verb second) – compare weil ich Durst habe.
denn never starts an answer: Warum? – Weil ich müde bin (not *Denn ich bin müde).
subtleties: In questions denn is a softening particle, not “because”: Was machst du denn?

profile.feeling: That’s why, so – it points back to the reason, and the verb follows at once.

examples.text: Ich habe Hunger, deshalb esse ich ein Brot.
examples.tr: I’m hungry, so I’m eating a sandwich.

examples.text: Es ist kalt, deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.tr: It’s cold, so we’re staying at home.

examples.text: Meine Familie wohnt in Wien. Deshalb lerne ich Deutsch.
examples.tr: My family lives in Vienna. That’s why I’m learning German.

synonyms.nuance: that’s why – the same, a little more spoken
therefore, hence
that’s why – also the childish answer Darum! (“Because!”)
so – a conclusion rather than a reason

etymology.text: From Middle High German deshalp, from Middle High German des, dez (“from that, therefore, thereon”) + halp (“half”).

funFacts: des is the old genitive “of that”: deshalb, deswegen and Greek γι’ αυτό (“for this”) all point back to the reason just given.
pitfalls: deshalb is an adverb, not a conjunction: it takes the first place and the verb follows at once – deshalb esse ich (not *deshalb ich esse).
subtleties: It can also stand after the verb: Ich esse deshalb ein Brot.
A comma (or a full stop) comes before it.

profile.feeling: That’s why, because of that – the spoken twin of deshalb.

examples.text: Es ist kalt, deswegen bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.tr: It’s cold, so we’re staying at home.

examples.text: Ich bin krank, deswegen komme ich heute nicht.
examples.tr: I’m ill, so I’m not coming today.

examples.text: Deswegen bin ich hier.
examples.tr: That’s why I’m here.

synonyms.nuance: the same – a little more neutral in writing
that’s why
hence

etymology.text: Univerbation of des (“the, that”) + wegen (“because of”), using postpositive wegen.

funFacts: Speakers use deshalb and deswegen interchangeably; deswegen sounds slightly more colloquial.
pitfalls: Like deshalb it takes the first place and the verb follows: deswegen bleiben wir (not *deswegen wir bleiben).
subtleties: deswegen = des + wegen (“because of that”); wegen alone is the preposition “because of” (wegen des Wetters).

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s adverb sense “then, thus, so, hence” is this concept (hence = therefore); it lists the same sense under its conjunction entry (“so, therefore”). German grammars class also as an adverb, because it takes the first place and the verb follows (also fahre ich).

profile.feeling: So, therefore – a conclusion; and the “well, so …” that starts a new thought. Not English “also”!

senses.def: so? then? (in questions: Kommst du also?)

examples.text: Der Bus ist langsam, also fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad.
examples.tr: The bus is slow, so I’ll go by bike.

examples.text: Ich denke, also bin ich.
examples.tr: I think, therefore I am.

examples.text: Also, was machen wir heute?
examples.tr: So, what are we doing today?

examples.text: Du kommst also morgen?
examples.tr: So you’re coming tomorrow?

phrases.meaning: There you go! – told you so

synonyms.nuance: that’s why – points back to the reason
consequently
hence, therefore

etymology.text: From Middle High German alles, from Old High German also, alsō (“as, like”); equivalent to all + so. Cognate with English also, as.

funFacts: also and English also come from the same all + so – the meanings went separate ways.
pitfalls: False friend: German also = “so, therefore”; English “also” is auch (S09).
In writing the verb follows at once: also fahre ich (speech sometimes says also ich fahre, after a short pause).

profile.feeling: Then – the next step; and “in that case”.

senses.def: then (in Bis dann! = see you then)

examples.text: Wir essen, dann gehen wir in den Park.
examples.tr: We eat, then we go to the park.

examples.text: Zuerst trinke ich Kaffee, dann gehe ich zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: First I drink coffee, then I go to work.

examples.text: Wenn du Hunger hast, dann iss etwas!
examples.tr: If you’re hungry, then eat something!

examples.text: Bis dann!
examples.tr: See you then!

phrases.meaning: ironic: well, good luck with that!

synonyms.nuance: after that – stresses the order
afterwards, subsequently
later

etymology.text: From Middle High German dann, from Old High German danne, from Proto-West Germanic *þan. Cognate with English then.

funFacts: dann is the twin of denn (because) – one word until the 18th century.
pitfalls: dann takes the first place and the verb follows: dann gehen wir (not *dann wir gehen).
“Then” = “at that time (in the past)” is damals, not dann: Damals war ich jung.
subtleties: In Wenn …, dann … the dann is optional: Wenn du Hunger hast, (dann) iss etwas.

profile.feeling: When and if – for the present, the future and every repeated time; the verb goes to the end.

senses.def: if only (a wish: Wenn ich doch …!)

examples.text: Ruf mich an, wenn du ankommst.
examples.tr: Call me when you arrive.

examples.text: Immer wenn ich nach Berlin fahre, besuche ich meine Tante.
examples.tr: Whenever I go to Berlin, I visit my aunt.

examples.text: Wenn ich Hunger habe, esse ich ein Brot.
examples.tr: If I’m hungry, I eat a sandwich.

examples.text: Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.tr: If it rains, we stay at home.

examples.text: Wenn ich doch nur Zeit hätte!
examples.tr: If only I had time!

phrases.text: Wenn das Wörtchen „wenn“ nicht wär, wär mein Vater Millionär.
phrases.tr: If the little word “if” weren’t there, my father would be a millionaire.

synonyms.nuance: in case, if – only for conditions
as soon as
when – only for one event or period in the past

etymology.text: From Middle High German wanne, wenne, from Old High German hwanne, hwenne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan, similar to the adverb wann.

funFacts: wenn, wann and English when are the same old word in different jobs.
pitfalls: wenn ≠ wann: wann is the question word (Wann kommst du?), wenn joins clauses (Wenn du kommst, …).
One event in the past is als, not wenn: Als ich jung war, … (wenn in the past only for “every time”).
“If” = “whether” after wissen, fragen is ob: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt (not *wenn).
The finite verb goes to the END of the clause: …, wenn ich Hunger habe.
subtleties: English if and when are both wenn in the present and future; context decides.
If the wenn-clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: Wenn es kalt ist, trinken wir Tee.

profile.feeling: If, whether – for an indirect yes/no question; the verb goes to the end.

examples.text: Ich weiß nicht, ob er heute kommt.
examples.tr: I don’t know if he’s coming today.

examples.text: Kannst du fragen, ob das Café offen ist?
examples.tr: Can you ask if the café is open?

examples.text: Ob das wohl stimmt?
examples.tr: I wonder if that’s true.

examples.text: Er sieht aus, als ob er müde wäre.
examples.tr: He looks as if he were tired.

profile.synonymsNone: No other word introduces an indirect yes/no question; wenn (if) is only for conditions.

etymology.text: From Middle High German obe, ob, from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”). Compare English if.

funFacts: ob and English if go back to the same Proto-Germanic word *jabai.
pitfalls: “if” = “whether” is ob: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt; “if” = a condition is wenn: Wenn er kommt, essen wir.
The finite verb goes to the END of the clause: …, ob er heute kommt.
subtleties: Ob …? alone is a wondering question: Ob er heute kommt? (I wonder if he’s coming today.)

profile.feeling: That – the conjunction that turns a sentence into a part of another: Ich bin froh, dass du hier bist.

examples.text: Ich bin froh, dass du hier bist.
examples.tr: I’m glad that you’re here.

examples.text: Ich weiß, dass das teuer ist.
examples.tr: I know that it’s expensive.

examples.text: Es ist schön, dass ihr kommt.
examples.tr: It’s nice that you’re coming.

examples.text: Sprich lauter, dass ich dich verstehe!
examples.tr: Speak louder so that I can understand you!

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: dass is the only “that” conjunction; the clause can be left without it (Ich glaube, er kommt).

etymology.text: From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Dutch dat, Low German dat, English that. Doublet of das. The distinction from das is purely an orthographical convention.

funFacts: dass and das are the same word – the spelling split is only a convention; before 1996 dass was written daß.
pitfalls: dass (conjunction, ss) vs das (article or pronoun, s): if you can replace it with dieses or welches, write das.
The finite verb goes to the END of the clause: …, dass du hier bist.
subtleties: Speech often drops dass and keeps main-clause order: Ich glaube, er kommt = Ich glaube, dass er kommt.

profile.feeling: Although – a contrast, with the verb at the end.

examples.text: Wir gehen in den Park, obwohl es kalt ist.
examples.tr: We’re going to the park although it’s cold.

examples.text: Obwohl sie müde ist, geht sie zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: Although she’s tired, she goes to work.

examples.text: Ich esse noch ein Stück, obwohl ich satt bin.
examples.tr: I’ll have another piece, although I’m full.

synonyms.nuance: although
nevertheless – an adverb, verb follows (Es ist kalt, trotzdem gehen wir)
even if, even though

etymology.text: Univerbation of ob + wohl, from the older use of ob as a conditional and concessive conjunction, reinforced with an adverb. Compare obgleich, obschon.

funFacts: obwohl = ob + wohl: the old “if” word plus wohl (well).
pitfalls: The finite verb goes to the END of the clause: …, obwohl es kalt ist.
obwohl joins (…, obwohl es kalt ist); trotzdem is an adverb with the verb next (Es ist kalt, trotzdem gehen wir).
subtleties: Speech sometimes uses obwohl as a correction with main-clause order: Ich komme mit – obwohl, nein, ich bin zu müde.
